title: Protecting groups and chemoselectivity
goal: Put a protecting group on, take it off again, and know what each one survives, then use the same ideas to join amino acids into peptides.

problemSets.title: Protecting alcohols
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Turn an OH into a silyl ether or an acetal; each comes off under its own conditions.
problemSets.conceptCard:
When a molecule has two groups that would both react, one can be **masked** for a while. A good protecting group goes on easily, survives the reactions that follow, and comes off cleanly under conditions that leave everything else alone.

Alcohols have two main families:

- **Silyl ethers** (TBS, TIPS, TBDPS): the oxygen attacks **silicon**, helped by imidazole. Silicon is large and can briefly hold **five groups**, so substitution there is easy even with three groups on it. The bulky tert-butyl group makes TBS go on a **primary** OH faster than a secondary one. **Fluoride** removes it: the Si–F bond is about 120 kJ mol⁻¹ stronger than Si–O
- **Acetals** (THP, MOM): the OH adds to an **oxocarbenium ion**, the same cation as in acetal formation from an aldehyde. Acetals survive base, Grignard reagents and hydrides, and come off with **aqueous acid**

So a molecule can carry a TBS ether and a THP ether, and either can be removed while the other stays: **orthogonal** protection.

The *p*-methoxybenzyl (PMB) ether, removed by DDQ, comes later: DDQ takes a single electron, which the app cannot draw yet.

setItems.whyThisOne: A reminder: an acetal forms through an oxocarbenium ion. THP and MOM use the same cation.
Imidazole carries the silyl group, and the primary OH wins.
Fluoride adds to silicon: five groups on one atom, for a moment.
Protonate an enol ether, and the alcohol adds to the cation.
An oxygen pushes chloride out of MOMCl; a hindered base mops up the acid.

problemSets.title: Protecting amines
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A carbamate ties up the nitrogen lone pair; Boc comes off with acid, Fmoc with base.
problemSets.conceptCard:
An amine is basic and nucleophilic. Turning it into a **carbamate** (R₂N–CO–OR) delocalises its lone pair into the C=O, as in an amide, so it no longer reacts. What changes is how the carbamate is removed:

- **Boc** (tert-butoxycarbonyl) goes on with Boc₂O and comes off with **acid** (TFA): the tert-butyl group leaves as a stable **tertiary cation**, and the carbamic acid loses **CO₂**
- **Fmoc** (9-fluorenylmethoxycarbonyl) comes off with **base** (piperidine): the fluorene C–H is acidic because its anion is **aromatic**, and an **E1cB** elimination follows

Boc survives base, Fmoc survives acid: the pair is **orthogonal**, which is the basis of solid-phase peptide synthesis.

The benzyl carbamate (Cbz), removed by hydrogen on palladium, comes later: the app does not draw reactions on transition metals yet.

setItems.whyThisOne: The amine attacks Boc₂O, and the alcohol in the same molecule is left alone.
Acid, a tertiary cation and two gases: why Boc comes off so cleanly.
An aromatic anion, an E1cB elimination, and a trap for dibenzofulvene.

problemSets.title: Peptide coupling
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Make the acid's OH into a leaving group, catch it as an active ester, then let the amine in.
problemSets.conceptCard:
An amine and a carboxylic acid only make a salt. To form an amide, the OH of the acid is first turned into a **leaving group** by a coupling reagent:

- **DCC** gives an O-acylisourea. It is so reactive that on its own it rearranges to an unreactive N-acylurea, or cyclises to an oxazolone and **racemises** the amino acid
- **HOBt** (or HOAt) catches it first, as an **active ester**: reactive enough to meet the amine, too mild for the side reactions
- **HATU** builds the OAt active ester in one reagent. The pyridine nitrogen of OAt holds the incoming amine by a hydrogen bond, so it couples fast

Each amino acid needs its **amine protected** (Boc or Fmoc) so that it cannot couple with itself, and the partner's **acid protected** (here as a methyl ester). The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so racemisation is explained but not drawn.

setItems.whyThisOne: A reminder: DCC turns the acid's OH into a leaving group.
HOBt catches the O-acylisourea before it can go wrong.
One reagent does both jobs: the OAt ester, from a carboxylate.
